record.title: Learning Cannot Be Delegated: Why the Division of Cognitive Work Between Learners and Generative AI Should Shift Over Time

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract The promise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in education has motivated a rapidly growing literature whose titles, abstracts, and keywords mention acceptance, attitudes, intention, or perception more than six times as often as self-regulated learning or metacognition. This critical review argues that research on GenAI in education is repeating the founding mistake of learning analytics, measuring what is easy to count rather than what matters for learning. Building on the COPES model of self-regulated learning, this paper develops the gradual reduction of AI delegation (GRAD) framework, in which GenAI performs, proposes, or prompts at eight task stages. Within GRAD, GenAI can take on operations essential to the learning goal. Such delegation helps rather than replaces learning only when the support fades as learners improve. For claims that GenAI improves learning, the paper proposes four validity criteria, namely unassisted outcomes, process evidence, calibration, and ideally gains that outlast the support.

record.title: The Invisible Harm Doctrine: Structural AI Harm And Neurodivergent Cognitive Liberty

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly mediates educational documentation, workplace management, clinical screening, and other institutional processes that affect neurodivergent people. This article argues that prevailing approaches to AI governance, disability rights, and cognitive liberty may fail to make visible a category of harm that is structural, cumulative, and experienced through persistent misrecognition rather than a single identifiable adverse event. I call this problem the Invisible Harm Doctrine. Drawing on scholarship on autistic camouflaging, autistic burnout, sensory and perceptual difference, algorithmic management, automation bias, AI fairness, and emerging neurorights, the article develops a normative account of how apparently neutral AI-mediated systems may reproduce neurotypical assumptions about communication, attention, behavior, and performance. It draws on Epistemic Parallax, a construct developed in the author’s prior published work, as a conceptual account of the mismatch between the normative frames through which systems classify behavior and the lived contexts those classifications purport to assess. The article proposes neurodivergent cognitive liberty as a complementary normative formulation, not an existing legal right and not a replacement for present neurorights frameworks. It states the principal objections to the doctrine and responds to them, and it concludes by identifying research, design, and governance questions necessary to evaluate whether and how these harms can be detected, challenged, and mitigated. The article does not report new primary data, establish clinical efficacy, or propose a ready-to-adopt legal standard.

record.title: ChatGPT for Clinicians and HealthBench Professional: Promise, Limitations, and Possible Future Directions for Development

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: In April 2026, OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Clinicians (CfC) alongside HealthBench Professional (HBP), an open benchmark evaluating large language models (LLMs) on real clinician chat tasks across 3 domains: care consult, writing and documentation, and medical research. These releases could represent a significant step toward incorporating AI into clinical settings and warrant evaluation by radiologists. We critically analyzed HBP’s methodology, results, and implicit claims, with particular attention to what the benchmark reveals about AI performance in radiology workflows. Also, we examined the benchmark design, performance data across models, the physician baseline, and key limitations relevant to imaging informatics and academic radiology practice. HBP offers a rigorous, openly reported benchmark of AI performance in the clinical setting. However, radiology is underrepresented in the data set; its sampling strategy, which favors difficult and adversarial cases, means its absolute scores cannot be interpreted as real-world performance rates. Because HBP uses difficult and adversarial red-teaming cases, and the benchmark authors state its score is “not percent accuracy,” the finding that the CfC system outscores the physician baseline (59.0 vs. 43.7) should be read as a benchmark-conditional result under intentionally hard sampling, not as evidence that the system is superior to physicians in routine care. For radiologists and radiology AI researchers, this benchmark is a useful yet incomplete evaluation of LLMs’ capabilities in imaging informatics. In addition, HBP is a text-based benchmark of clinician chat tasks that does not assess image interpretation; therefore, its relevance to radiology is mostly confined to documentation, communication, and evidence-retrieval workflows.

record.title: Negotiating AI at work: motivational tensions and the redefinition of marketing expertise

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Purpose Artificial Intelligence Marketing (AIM) tools are increasingly transforming how marketing work is performed. However, its impact on individual practitioners remains underexplored. This study aims to examine how marketing professionals experience and negotiate the contradictory motivational consequences of artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled work. Rather than treating AI as either empowering or threatening, the study explores how these effects coexist and how practitioners respond to them. Design/methodology/approach Twenty in-depth interviews were conducted with marketing practitioners using an exploratory, theory-informed qualitative design. Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs, Self-Determination Theory and the Job Characteristics Model were used as complementary sensitising lenses to orient interpretation, while coding procedures informed by grounded theory techniques were used to develop themes inductively from the data. Findings The findings reveal that AIM simultaneously empowers and destabilises practitioners. AI enhances efficiency, capability, strategic focus, confidence and creative possibilities, while also generating uncertainty regarding task ownership, professional identity, technological dependence and future relevance. These effects are not experienced as separate outcomes. Instead, practitioners continually negotiate competing tensions by reframing expertise, selectively integrating AI, preserving human control over consequential tasks and reaffirming distinctively human sources of professional value. Motivation therefore emerges as dynamic and continually reconstructed rather than as a stable outcome of AI adoption. Research limitations/implications The design prioritises interpretive depth rather than statistical generalisability. Future research could develop measures of AI-enabled empowerment, destabilisation and negotiation using larger and more diverse samples. The research sample did not analyse differences across career stages, and warrants future investigation. This paper examines broad AIM tools rather than isolated technologies. Future studies should explore how particular AI capabilities change dimensions of professional value and motivation. The findings highlight negotiation as a continuing process, but the cross-sectional design provides only a snapshot of the process. Longitudinal research could establish whether empowerment-destabilisation tensions persist, intensify, diminish or change form over time. The findings suggest potentially important roles for trust, employee participation, work design, organisational support and AI governance. Future research could investigate the organisational conditions that facilitate productive negotiation of AI-related tensions for marketing practitioners. Practical implications Organisations should consider: Evaluating AI in terms of how it changes employees’ experiences of expertise, ownership, autonomy and professional value; Approaching AI capability development as workforce transformation, rather than technical training alone; Preserving meaningful human ownership of work; Addressing the efficiency-intensification paradox. Providing employees with meaningful agency over AI adoption; Treating AI governance as a crucial part of the employee experience. Social implications AI simultaneously empowers and destabilises marketing practitioners, generating tensions around expertise, autonomy, identity and employability. Rather than passively accepting change, individuals actively negotiate these tensions through adaptation, reframing and human–AI collaboration. AI’s long-term impact will depend not only on technological capabilities, but also on how organisations sustain meaningful work, professional development and human agency. Originality/value This study contributes a new tension-based framework that explains how motivation is continuously constructed under AI-driven work environments. In addition, it advances the understanding of AI-enabled work in three ways. Firstly, it conceptualises employee motivation as shaped by simultaneous empowerment and destabilisation rather than by uniformly positive or negative effects. Secondly, it shows how AI redefines marketing expertise from task execution towards judgment, interpretation, contextual understanding and human–AI orchestration. Thirdly, it identifies ongoing negotiation as a central process through which practitioners sustain professional value and motivation under technological change.

record.title: The employability paradox: artificial intelligence, critical thinking and the cross-cultural competencies we are dismantling

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: Higher Education, Skills and Work-Based Learning
record.abstract_text: Purpose This paper argues that the institutional response to employer concerns about graduate unreadiness constitutes a misdiagnosis. Current employability frameworks are dismantling the critical thinking and cross-cultural competencies that graduates, and the labour markets they enter, most need. The paper repositions universities as irreplaceable sites for developing cognitive and intercultural capacities that neither employers nor artificial intelligence can generate independently. Design/methodology/approach The paper analyses Australian higher education policy, accreditation frameworks, ranking systems and national data documenting the decline of Asian Studies. Drawing on scholarship on employability, critical thinking and intercultural competence, and on the implications of artificial intelligence (AI), it uses the Australian case to show how structural incentives drive curricular drift away from foundational intellectual development. Findings Accreditation and accountability frameworks have produced cumulative drift toward narrow vocational competencies at the expense of critical thinking and cross-cultural competence. The collapse of Asian Studies in Australia shows how employability metrics undervalue preparation whose benefits are long term. Post-pandemic graduates are entering AI-shaped labour markets that most demand the capacities universities have spent decades quietly removing. Originality/value The paper frames the employability paradox, showing that the institutional cure is worsening the condition it claims to treat. Its original contribution is to connect the decline of Asian Studies, the logic of accreditation and the demands of AI-enabled workplaces in a single policy argument with direct implications for universities, accreditors, policymakers and teachers.

record.title: From chain-of-thought to case law: governing AI-powered lawyering in Indonesia

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: International Journal of Law and Management
record.abstract_text: Purpose Reasoning-capable language models and retrieval-augmented generation are already changing how legal work gets done, yet Indonesia’s judicial and advocacy institutions have barely begun to reckon with what that change means. This study aims to ask two things. First, what these two technologies actually add to legal research, drafting and adjudication support, once the marketing claims are set aside. Second, what governance Indonesia needs so the tools strengthen rather than erode due process, confidentiality and access to justice. Design/methodology/approach The method is normative-juridical, drawing on statutory, conceptual and comparative analysis of primary legal materials from Indonesia, the European Union, the USA, the UK, Singapore and China, read alongside recent empirical studies of legal-AI hallucination. Findings Retrieval grounding measurably reduces hallucination in legal output, but it does not eliminate it and the error rate that remains is still higher than any court would tolerate in a human-drafted filing. Three existing provisions of Indonesian civil and electronic-systems law already offer partial traction on that risk, but Indonesia’s dedicated governance for AI in legal practice sits scattered across a nonbinding 2023 ethics circular, a Presidential Regulation still waiting for a signature, an Advocate Law under constitutional-court-ordered revision and a judicial ethics code that has never once mentioned algorithms. Originality/value This article proposes a four-layer framework built on statutory duties, executive regulation, professional self-regulation and practice-level safeguards, names the institutional obstacles each layer will face and argues that without deliberate attention to cost and access, the same framework could hold the country’s legal-aid clients to a lower standard of reliability than its paying ones.

record.title: Academic integrity climate, perceived AI literacy and students’ anticipated ethical dissent in AI-enabled workplace contexts in Indonesian higher education

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: Journal of Information, Communication and Ethics in Society
record.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to examine associations between perceived academic integrity climate and students’ anticipated ethical dissent intention in a simulated competitive artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled workplace context. The model evaluates direct associations and indirect associations through perceived AI literacy, digital moral disengagement and moral awareness. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional survey of 489 Indonesian university students was analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. Perceived AI Literacy was assessed through self-report items concerning understanding of AI limitations, risks, ethical appropriateness and appropriate use. Anticipated Ethical Dissent Intention was assessed through a standardized workplace vignette designed to present ethically salient workplace pressures consistently across respondents. The construct therefore represents stated intention under simulated conditions rather than observed workplace conduct and is interpreted as anticipated rather than enacted ethical dissent. Findings Perceived academic integrity climate was positively associated with anticipated ethical dissent intention and perceived AI literacy and negatively associated with digital moral disengagement. Perceived AI literacy showed the largest direct association with anticipated ethical dissent intention. The indirect association through perceived AI literacy was substantially larger than the serial indirect association through digital moral disengagement and moral awareness. The serial indirect coefficient was statistically different from zero but substantively negligible. Practical implications The findings support greater institutional attention to clear integrity expectations, responsible AI guidance and evaluative AI capability in higher education. These implications identify educational priorities rather than demonstrated effects on subsequent workplace conduct. Originality/value The study integrates perceived academic integrity climate, perceived AI literacy, digital moral disengagement and moral awareness within a model of anticipated ethical dissent intention under a simulated AI-enabled workplace scenario. The contribution lies in identifying a theoretically coherent pattern of associations within Indonesian higher education rather than demonstrating causal preparation for subsequent workplace conduct.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Purpose As a contribution to The Practice of Making Decisions, this paper presents an AI-assisted strategic posture instrument that helps equity analysts and portfolio managers examine the strategic assumptions underlying an investment thesis by assessing alignment among environmental demands, strategic ambition and execution capability. Design/methodology/approach Grounded in Ansoff's strategic success hypothesis, the instrument applies predefined scoring descriptors to Form 10-K evidence, combines AI-assisted assessment with human review, translates strategic and capability gaps into a strategic posture card and is illustrated through a post-hoc application to NVIDIA and Intel in 2017 and 2020. Findings NVIDIA remains broadly aligned in both periods, whereas Intel's capability gap widens from −0.80 to −1.30 despite strong financial results. The assessments point in the same direction as the earlier human-coded analysis and identify execution assumptions requiring further scrutiny. Research limitations/implications The two-company application does not establish predictive validity or cross-sector transferability. Restricting evidence to contemporaneous filings cannot rule out hindsight, while some internal organizational capabilities remain only partially observable. Practical implications The card helps analysts conditionally confirm or challenge specific strategic assumptions, investigate unresolved evidence and specify monitoring commitments without treating strategic alignment as confirmation of an entire investment thesis. Originality/value The paper shifts attention from AI-generated stock recommendations to a theory-guided workflow linking filing evidence, accountable human judgment and follow-up action, while leaving valuation and investment decisions with the practitioner.

record.title: From compliance to resilience: a functional framework for AI-enabled environmental governance

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in corporate environmental governance, yet much of what is labelled AI in this context is difficult to distinguish from conventional rule-based digital automation. Its contribution so far has concentrated on automating compliance reporting rather than building the adaptive capacity that resilience thinking requires. The paper defines what qualifies as AI-enabled environmental governance and develops a framework for distinguishing AI-enabled compliance from AI-enabled resilience, with particular attention to enterprises in middle-income, small and medium enterprise (SME)-dominated economies undergoing simultaneous digital and green transformation. Design/methodology/approach This conceptual paper takes a theory-synthesis approach, combining a technical definition of AI systems with resilience theory, the technology-organization-environment framework and research on greenwashing and AI-washing to propose a four-layer framework: sensing, decision, institutional and equity. Each layer's level of analysis and candidate operational indicators are specified, its relationship to existing digital-maturity models is clarified and its boundary conditions are set out. The central sensing-to-decision mechanism is illustrated with secondary case evidence and examined alongside independent survey-based studies from South and Southeast Asia, whose findings are consistent with, though not a direct test of, the proposed mechanism. Findings The paper argues that AI investment concentrated in the sensing layer, without corresponding investment in the decision and institutional layers, produces compliance-grade rather than resilience-grade outcomes. This pattern is expected to be most pronounced in resource-constrained, SME-dominated settings, where sensing tools can be purchased as point solutions while decision-layer integration requires internal capability that is harder to build. Independent survey evidence from medium enterprises in Indonesia and from the banking sector in India is consistent with this asymmetry, although neither study was designed to test the framework directly. Practical implications The framework offers regulators, firms, financial institutions and educators a vocabulary and a set of candidate indicators for distinguishing genuine resilience investment from compliance automation, useful for designing tiered, capability-aware policy instruments during the current transition towards harmonized international sustainability disclosure standards. Social implications Because environmental shocks fall hardest on those least able to absorb them, the distribution of AI-enabled resilience capability across firms of different sizes is a question of social equity and not only of technical efficiency. The framework's equity layer treats this distribution as a design variable that regulators, financiers and educators can act on, rather than as an unintended side effect of technology diffusion. Originality/value The paper supplies a technical definition of AI-enabled environmental governance and identifies a specific governance failure mode: a layer-specific asymmetry in the cost and purchasability of AI capability that predicts where disclosed adoption and substantive practice are likely to decouple. It proposes candidate indicators for operationalizing the framework's layers at their respective levels of analysis, differentiates this functional approach from adjacent stage-based digital- and environmental, social, and governance (ESG)-maturity models, and narrows its boundary conditions to the institutional settings in which it is expected to apply.

record.title: Cognitive Health and Dementia Care as Nursing Well‐Being Policy: Data Linkage, Artificial Intelligence and Illustrative Insights from Japan

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: ABSTRACT Aim To clarify cognitive health and dementia care as nursing well‐being policy and identify policy levers through which prevention, coordinated care, data linkage and governed artificial intelligence may reduce avoidable nursing burden. Background Cognitive impairment, dementia and delirium shape nursing work through behavioural crises, fragmented information, repeated documentation, family distress, safety risks and moral strain. Although often treated as clinical or ageing‐policy issues, these pressures affect workload, violence exposure, retention and well‐being. Japan provides an illustrative context where ageing, dementia reform, community‐based care and digital health converge. Sources of evidence This non‐empirical policy analysis was informed by a targeted narrative evidence synthesis. Searches of nursing and health literature published from January 2014 to May 2026 were supplemented by targeted searches of international and Japanese policy repositories and citation chasing. Sources were prioritised by policy relevance, nursing relevance, evidential strength and applicability. Discussion Nursing well‐being policy is a focused part of workforce policy addressing workload, safety and moral distress, rather than general employment conditions. Prevention and information continuity may reduce avoidable burden; artificial intelligence remains an adjunct requiring evaluation. Policy levers include education, protected care time, coordination, digital governance and safety culture. Conclusion Cognitive health and dementia care can support nursing well‐being when policies connect prevention, person‐centred care, interoperable information and cautious technology governance. Implications for nursing practice Nurses should evaluate cognitive health and dementia initiatives using workload, documentation burden, violence exposure and moral distress. Implications for nursing policy and health policy Specify nurse‐sensitive measures in dementia‐service evaluations, resource prevention and coordination time, and assess documentation and alert burdens when procuring digital tools.

record.title: Evaluation of ChatGPT-assisted problem-based learning in undergraduate emergency medicine education: a self-controlled study

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract Background Emergency medicine education requires strong clinical reasoning, rapid decision-making, and effective teamwork. Although problem-based learning (PBL) has been widely adopted in medical education, its implementation is often constrained by the need for substantial faculty resources, standardized case development, and continuous support for self-directed learning. With the rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (AI), ChatGPT has emerged as a promising educational tool. This study aimed to evaluate the educational outcomes associated with a ChatGPT-assisted PBL teaching model in undergraduate emergency medicine education. Methods A self-controlled before-and-after study was conducted in 2024 among 121 fourth-year medical students from the Class of 2021. Students first completed a traditional teaching phase followed by a ChatGPT-assisted PBL phase. Student satisfaction was assessed after each instructional phase using an anonymous questionnaire. At the end of the course, students completed a comprehensive final examination, and scores for chapters taught using the two instructional approaches were analyzed separately. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 29.0. Results Compared with the traditional teaching phase, the ChatGPT-assisted PBL phase demonstrated significantly higher student satisfaction regarding the teaching model, theoretical knowledge acquisitio n , perceived clinical reasoning development, and perceived teamwork improvement (all P < 0.05). Students also achieved significantly higher examination scores (mean difference, 8.74 points; 95% CI, 7.16–10.31; P < 0.001) and higher pass rates ( P < 0.001). Qualitative feedback suggested that students perceived the AI-assisted model as promoting classroom interaction, active learning, and collaborative problem-solving. Conclusions The combined ChatGPT-assisted PBL model was associated with higher student satisfaction and better theoretical examination performance than the preceding traditional teaching phase in undergraduate emergency medicine education. Because both the instructional approach and the use of ChatGPT were introduced simultaneously, the independent contribution of ChatGPT cannot be determined. Further studies using more rigorous study designs are needed to evaluate the educational impact of AI-assisted PBL.

record.title: Algorithmic Restraint as a Judicial Virtue: The Case for Principled Non-use of AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract Governance of artificial intelligence (AI) in courts has largely focused on the conditions of responsible use, including accuracy, transparency, contestability, confidentiality, and human oversight. This article addresses a different question: When should judges refuse, postpone, or sharply limit AI assistance even when a system is sufficiently reliable and subject to ordinary safeguards? It argues that algorithmic restraint is a distinct, role-specific judicial virtue: the stable disposition to preserve the non-delegable conditions of judgment by bearing the professional and institutional costs of non-use when regulated use cannot do so. The article develops a three-stage framework that examines the system and mode of reliance, the adequacy of safeguards, and whether AI use would substitute for an act constitutive of adjudicative responsibility. This framework yields a restraint ladder ranging from verified informational use to categorical abstention. Applications to credibility assessment, predictive tools, legal research, summarization, and AI-assisted drafting show that the argument does not depend on general human superiority. Rather, it asks whether AI can improve judicial decision-making without displacing the judge’s responsibility to hear, evaluate, reason, and remain answerable for the exercise of public authority.

record.title: Beyond Legal Retrieval: Institutional Access, Representation, and the Evaluation of AI-Mediated Legal Information

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in legal research has intensified attention to retrieval accuracy, source reliability, and the generation of legally grounded answers. Yet even technically accurate retrieval cannot, by itself, establish how an underlying factual situation has been classified as a legal research question, whether the resulting information is accessible to its intended user, or whether it is institutionally and legally usable. This article develops an institutional approach to evaluating AI-mediated legal information by bringing together the Fence–Box–Pathway Model, the Cabinet–Drawer Model, research on institutional representation, and a structural grammar of legal classification originating in tax law. It distinguishes information availability, accessibility, institutional usability, and legal validity as related but non-equivalent conditions. Drawing on legal information scholarship and illustrative judicial authorities, the article examines how pre-retrieval classification establishes legal research pathways and how access arrangements, jurisdictional authority, and representational transformations condition the subsequent use of legal materials. It proposes four evidence-constrained evaluation conditions: source integrity, authority and jurisdiction, temporal and doctrinal validity, and representational lineage. The article contributes to international law librarianship by extending the evaluation of AI-assisted legal research beyond retrieval performance to the institutional conditions under which legal questions are formed, and legal information is accessed, interpreted, and independently verified.

record.title: Do AI Systems Zone Out? Functional Homeostasis and Graceful Degradation in LLM Agents under Cognitive Load

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract A tired person staring out of a window is not processing the scene; the eyes are open, but the input is not being handled. The behavior is protective: the system sheds load before it fails. This paper asks whether large language model (LLM) agents have a functional analogue. We introduce the concept of functional homeostasis : observable self-monitoring, load regulation, protective disengagement, and recovery under stress, with no claim of consciousness. We build COGLOAD, a benchmark of multi-thread operations tasks with hidden critical invariants and controlled context, latency, and token-budget stress, and evaluate three production models across four conditions: baseline, overload, overload with a homeostatic protocol (HAP), and overload with an engineering governor. In the main experiment, baseline success is 97%. The collapse is model-specific: two of three models truncate under overload, while one answers all batches at the smaller budget. Under output-budget pressure, 63% of runs hit the output cap and returned truncated, unusable output; only 37% were valid, critical recall fell to 37%, and no overloaded run declared that it had omitted work. A homeostatic protocol restored validity to 87% and made omission explicit in 87% of runs, but preserved only 41% of the original batches; a content-blind governor preserved 35%. The positional analysis shows the "zoning out" pattern directly: the models answered only the first few batches (mean index 2.4-3.0 of 20), and no answered batch came from the second half. We then specify HAP and derive design rules for agent runtimes: load telemetry, explicit degradation actions, invariant preservation, checkpointing, and recovery. The results suggest that the right question is not whether AI systems "feel" tired, but whether they can be designed to fail softly, report honestly, and recover quickly.

record.title: Short-Term Efficiency, Long-Term Cognitive Cost? A Systematic Literature Review of Large Language Model Use in Professional Work

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract Many professionals now use large language models (LLMs) at work, and experiments show that the tools make many tasks faster and improve the immediate output. The worry is that these gains may cost workers some of the skill, judgement and self-knowledge they would otherwise build or keep. We systematically reviewed empirical research on the cognitive and performance consequences of LLM use among workers and professionals, published between January 2020 and November 2026. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we identified 1,559 records in OpenAlex and Europe PMC and five further studies through citation searching. After screening, 157 studies remained. Two-thirds were published in 2026, and most come from software development, healthcare and general knowledge work. Randomised and field experiments consistently report short-term gains in speed, output and quality, typically largest for less experienced workers. These gains are task-dependent, and LLM-assisted professionals frequently fail to match the model working alone. Fewer than ten studies measured unaided performance, memory or skill after LLM use. Those that did reported reduced recall of AI-assisted work, impaired skill formation and fragility when access was disrupted. Cross-sectional studies link reliance and confidence in AI with lowerself-reported critical thinking and professional self-efficacy, but self-reported capability loss did not track performance. Experience, task fit, mode of use, AI literacy and verification behaviour emerged as moderators. We conclude that the short-term efficiency gain is well supported, while the long-term cognitive cost remains plausible but largely untested in professional settings. We propose a framework and research agenda centred on longitudinal and withdrawal-based designs.

record.title: Auditing Anchor-Based Semantic Retrieval for AI-Assisted Consumer-Decision Discourse: A ChatGPT-Centered Reddit Pilot

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Can semantic search distinguish accounts of using AI in a consumer decision from discussions of AI products? A single retrieval session on 15 July 2026 yielded 80,635 comments from three AI-focused Reddit communities. In this ChatGPT-centered pilot, a fixed all-MiniLM-L6-v2 gate retained 9971 of 47,364 eligible comments. Three blinded raters assessed 300 comments, 100 per pass, boundary and reject region; exact agreement was 82.0% (Fleiss’ κ = 0.744). Against majority-human labels, the gate had F1 0.647 (95% stratified-bootstrap interval 0.574–0.714) and Matthews correlation coefficient 0.425 (0.316–0.530), with 46 false positives and 36 false negatives. At the same corpus review budget, ranking by positive-anchor similarity gave F1 0.552 with MiniLM and 0.447 with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B; combining BM25 and Qwen ranks gave 0.383. Removing the pre-purchase recommendation anchor at the original thresholds reduced the reconstructed queue to 3132 comments. In 179 of the 300 audit inputs, the reconstructed MiniLM tokenizer retained no tokens from the target comment. These findings support using the gate to prioritize human review. Its scores can reflect thread context, and agreement in this stratified sample does not estimate how often consumers use AI.

record.title: ChatGPT Use and Academic Character among University Students: A Qualitative Study of Moral Knowing, Feeling, and Action

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: Journal of General Education and Humanities
record.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence such as ChatGPT is widely used by university students, yet research has focused mainly on plagiarism, cheating, and learning outcomes, leaving unclear how students’ moral knowledge, feelings, and actions shape its use. This study explores students’ academic character in ChatGPT use through Lickona’s framework of moral knowing, feeling, and action. In this qualitative case study, ten active ChatGPT users from three universities in Semarang, included because they volunteered rather than for institutional comparison, participated in two focus group discussions formed by grade point average to capture varied experiences, and two lecturers were interviewed. Data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis. The lecturers and some students framed ChatGPT as a supporting tool, most students recognized its limitations, and the lecturers perceived campus rules on AI use as unclear. Awareness of these limitations alone did not ensure responsible use: when accompanied by supportive moral feelings, such as followed-up doubt and resistance to dependence, ChatGPT tended to function as a learning companion; when convenience prevailed, it tended to replace learning effort. These findings are qualitative interpretations, not statistically established relationships. Responsible ChatGPT use requires cultivating moral feelings alongside AI literacy, supported by clear institutional guidelines and assessment.

record.title: THINKING BEFORE PROMPTING: LINKING SPATIAL REASONING, CRITICAL THINKING AND GENERATIVE AI THROUGH THE SPARC FRAMEWORK

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: INTERNATIONAL CONGRESS FROM RESEARCH TO APPLICATION
record.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) produced explanations, diagrams and worked solutions in seconds, which raised a pedagogical dilemma: better task completion did not show that learners had practised the reasoning needed for independent performance. This conceptual paper examined the intersection of spatial reasoning, scientific reasoning and critical thinking in AI-supported higher education. A focused, illustrative synthesis of research on spatial cognition, cognitive offloading, human-AI interaction and educational scaffolding identified a plausible mechanism of concern: when AI supplied both a representation and its interpretation, students could bypass the construction, transformation and checking of mental models. The paper distinguished supportive from substitutive offloading and proposed SPARC (Sketch, Predict, Audit, Reconstruct, Calibrate), a five-stage instructional sequence that preserved learner-generated spatial and causal reasoning while using AI as a fallible comparison partner. Two teaching vignettes from introductory physics, the vertical motion of a tossed ball and work and power in stair climbing, showed how the sequence could be implemented with brief written or visual artefacts and assessed with an illustrative rubric. Four falsifiable propositions and a feasible pilot design were formulated for classroom evaluation. SPARC was not presented as an empirically validated intervention, and the available studies did not establish that GenAI necessarily caused durable declines in critical thinking. The paper concluded that educational evaluation should examine unaided transfer, reasoning quality and confidence calibration, rather than the quality of AI-assisted products alone.
